extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, epistemology, and philosophy of science (readers studying induction and causation)
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual/theoretical account of causation used as the foundation for inductive reasoning: defines 'cause', distinguishes kinds of conditions, and gives principles for when an observed regularity counts as causal. Intended to guide rigorous treatment and identification of causal relations in scientific and philosophical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Causation (universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law of Causation: 'The truth that every fact which has a beginning has a cause' — a law co-extensive with human experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law is singled out as the fundamental law of succession suitable for forming the basis of rules for inductive logic. It is universal in that 'all instances whatever of succession' are examples of it, and recognition of it permits the expectation that a law will be found if we know how to find it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Cause (invariable and unconditional antecedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause is 'the antecedent, or the concurrence of antecedents, on which [a phenomenon] is invariably and unconditionally consequent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invariable sequence alone does not suffice; the antecedent must be believed to be followed by the consequent 'as long as the present constitution of things endures' (i.e., not merely observed to have followed in past experience). This distinguishes genuine causes from derivative or conditional sequences (example: day and night are not causes of one another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as the Whole Set of Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophically, the cause is 'the sum total of the conditions, positive and negative taken together' — the whole assemblage of contingencies whose realization makes the consequent invariable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accurate, one should enumerate all conditions (positive and negative) required for the effect. In practice some conditions are omitted if they are understood or irrelevant to the immediate purpose, but such omission yields an incomplete causal statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs Negative Conditions and Practical Subsumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative conditions of an event (absence of preventing or counteracting causes) may be numerous but can usually be summed under 'the absence of preventing or counteracting causes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because causes can counteract one another, negative conditions can be treated as an understood common proviso; the notion of cause can thus be limited to the assemblage of positive conditions 'subject to no other than negative conditions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate Event vs. Remote Conditions (selection of 'the cause')
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common to single out the proximate antecedent event as 'the cause' while treating other antecedent states (which may have lasted indefinitely) as mere conditions, but philosophically this selection is arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calling eating a dish the cause of death when in fact a combination (including bodily constitution, health, atmosphere) was required; or calling a last action the cause because it completes the set. Scientific accuracy requires recognizing the full concurrence of antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent and Patient Distinction is Verbal, Not Fundamental
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual distinction between an agent (that which acts) and a patient (that which is acted upon) is largely verbal; both are conditions and both contribute actively in causal sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: stone and earth both contribute in gravitation; patient attributes (organism's properties) actively shape the effect (e.g., prussic acid and the vital properties of the person). Thus causal description should treat all positive conditions as agents where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation by Production of Dispositions or Capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a class of causal relations where the effect is to confer a property or a capacity on an object (a 'state of preparation') which later enables it to produce another effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gunpowder's preparation for explosion; painting a wall conferring the property of producing a white sensation; education conferring capacities in the mind. In causal analysis, the immediate conditions of the final effect include the presence of objects possessing those properties, while the earlier causes produced those properties (conditions of conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible Omission of Conditions in Ordinary Language
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary discourse it is often acceptable to name one conspicuous condition as 'the cause' and omit others which are understood or immaterial to the present purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying a man's death was caused by his foot slipping (omitting his weight), or that legislative assent makes a bill law (omitting preceding conditions). Such shorthand is usage-dependent but scientifically incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Conditional from Unconditional Sequences by Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: We judge whether a uniform sequence is conditional or unconditional on experiential grounds; experience can show that one uniformity depends on other antecedents (so it is conditional) while another is unconditional (so causal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: We experimentally know the sun causes day (if the sun were always above horizon, day would persist); thus experience supports treating the sun's presence as the true cause and the night/day sequence as derivative. The criterion for causation includes the belief in necessity (unconditionalness) as grounded in experience.
